hints.hint: For puzzles where agents announce ignorance, write down exactly what each agent knows. If the setup leaves ambiguous which of two quantities was revealed, that ambiguity is part of every agent's uncertainty: never branch on "suppose it is the sum" versus "suppose it is the product". Pinning one reading makes every branch contradictory, so if you keep concluding "impossible", that is the bug. Merge both readings into one list: an agent holding x who sees N keeps every partner value legal under either reading (N-x, and N/x when it is a natural number). "I do not know" means at least two partner values survive, constraining that agent's own number. Apply announcements in order, filtering the previous survivors, without relitigating. Check one candidate makes both announcements true and no rival does, then report exactly one value and stop.

The edit turns that passive warning into an executable merged-candidate-list move and adds a concrete tripwire (repeated "impossible" means the knowledge model is wrong), while leaving the proven announcement-filtering and commit-and-stop clauses intact.

hints.hint: Whenever an equation equates two n-th powers of linear expressions in z, take moduli before hunting roots. FIRST MOVE: from (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, divide by (z-b)^n to get ((z-a)/(z-b))^n = c, then take moduli: |z-a| = k|z-b|. TRAP: k is the n-th ROOT of |c|, not |c| raised to the n-th power; verify k^n = |c| first, since a wrong k gives a self-consistent but wrong circle. Then set z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 terms, divide by their coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius (k=1 gives a line). Check numerically against the ORIGINAL equation, never your derived one: build one explicit root and measure its distance to your center. Report exactly one value, then stop.

hints.hint: Covered area = sum of areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Fix coordinates once, with the shared point at the origin, and never re-derive that setup. Key pruning: only the two edges meeting at the shared point can cut the small square; the far edges are too distant to matter, so the overlap is a right-angle wedge. Never conclude the small square is wholly covered; the wedge apex sits at its center. Then be numeric, not qualitative: for one angle, find where the two rays exit the square, list the polygon vertices in order, and shoelace it. Repeat for a second angle. If the two values agree, the overlap is angle-independent; never argue minimality in prose. Trust the shoelace numbers over any closed-form guess, never restart, and once a number is in hand do not re-derive it or write a formatted solution: state that one value in one short line and stop.
hints.mutation: cut unused proof/minimization clauses, add explicit no-rewrite termination rule

hints.hint:
Several hidden degree-n polynomials must jointly hit prescribed values at consecutive integers. Do not assume each polynomial is used only once.

Method: write the prescribed value as a function of the INPUT, not the position; for an arithmetic progression the target is then affine, L(x)=px+q. Fix one polynomial P and set g=P-L. Every input assigned to P is a root of g. Comparing degrees, g is not identically zero, so g has AT MOST n roots; that caps how many inputs one polynomial can serve. Off-by-one trap: the cap is n, not the interpolation count n+1. Multiply that cap over the family, then exhibit disjoint blocks where each polynomial interpolates L. Never shrink a count you already justified; report one exact integer, then stop.

hints.hint:
When unknown points on a fixed curve y=g(x) are tied by a known displacement (u,v), reduce to ONE unknown: let the free vertex be (t, g(t)) and its partner (t+u, g(t)+v), then solve the single scalar equation g(t+u) = g(t) + v.

For a logarithmic curve, convert that additive offset to a multiplicative one BEFORE cross-multiplying: log_c(B) - log_c(A) = v means B/A = c^v. Flipping the direction or sign of that power is the dominant failure mode.

If you hit an impossible identity or a negative discriminant, some ratio is inverted: numerically test g at a GIVEN point and fix only the line that fails to reproduce it. Never restart from scratch.

Discard roots reproducing a given vertex (degenerate). Finish with the shoelace determinant in cyclic order, then stop.

hints.hint: Describe a configuration by the ordered contents of the truck, gate, and shed rather than by informal move sequences. Each stack is last-in-first-out, so translate the asked-about position into a timing claim: whatever is deposited first sits at the bottom, and if the first delivery follows exactly k intake moves then that item is the k-th from the top of the original stack. Solve for the required k, then trace only the move sequences realizing that event, multiplying 1/2 per step where two moves were genuinely available and nothing where only one was possible; add those path probabilities. Do not claim each item is equally likely to occupy each position; the distribution over orders is not uniform. Report exactly one value per part, then stop.

hints.hint: Read the unknowns as weights of a functional L(f) = sum of weight_i times f(node_i) over distinct nodes - weights, not coefficients of a polynomial in x. The vanishing conditions say L kills a consecutive block of monomials; the last fixes L on one more. Note which monomial is NOT prescribed (often the constant) and keep it out of your test polynomial. First move: build ONE product vanishing at every node but the target one; evaluate L on it twice - by linearity, and as the target weight times its value at that node. Solve that one equation. Do not expand coefficients, chase harmonic sums, or test a small analogue. Reduce the product of node differences to a factorial, commit to one value, and stop reasoning.

hints.hint: Let n be the number of identical units the given totals split across. Integer per-unit stage costs force n to divide every listed stage total, so take n as their gcd unless the wording forbids it. Sum all cost components before dividing by n, apply any stated markup multiplicatively, and check integrality and units. Then report exactly one value and stop.

hints.hint: When the constraint is a commuting identity like p(q(x)) = q(p(x)) with unknown coefficients, do not expand the composition: its degree is the product of the degrees, and drowning in that algebra is the main way these problems are lost. Instead posit the affine link q = -p + k, using a fresh letter k that is never also a coefficient name of p, and fix k from the given point values. The identity then collapses to p(-p+k) = -p(p)+k; match coefficients from the highest degree downward, pinning the leading coefficient first. Never substitute one numeric x in place of coefficient matching - one point cannot determine the polynomial and silently yields wrong coefficients. Expect one leftover free coefficient; verify the requested outputs do not depend on it, then set it conveniently. Evaluate each requested output through q = -p + k rather than re-expanding q term by term. Recheck the given values once, then report one result and stop.

hints.hint: First move: for the two smallest sizes, write positions 0..N-1 as an explicit list and rewrite the whole list after each stage k=0,1,...,n-1 in order; all stages together are one operation. Once you trust the stages, switch to the cheap version: follow a single label's position through the n stages to get one index map, then iterate that map alone until it returns to start; that cycle length is your candidate order, and do not rewrite full lists again. Trap: the stages overlap, so the composite is not a product of disjoint swaps and usually is not its own inverse; never assert order 2 unless your trace confirms it. If a formula and a trace disagree, trust the trace. Budget rule: trace at most two sizes, never restart the analysis, and once two sizes agree report exactly one closed form in n, then stop.
hints.mutation: replace costly full-list re-verification clause with a single-label index map plus a two-size budget cap
